source.title: On Pre-training of Multimodal Language Models Customized for Chart Understanding
source.authors: Wan-Cyuan Fan; Yen-Chun Chen; Meng-Chen Liu; Lu Yuan; Leonid Sigal

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares downstream benchmark scores for 7B and 13B versions of its model, a different measure from the held-out loss scaling laws. It does not measure loss or fit scaling curves.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports ChartQA scores for the 7B and 13B models, which bear on downstream performance across model size. Other results, including training-data ablations, do not test the claim versions about scaling, allocation, or loss.
record.test_reason: This is a chart-understanding MLLM training paper. It fits no scaling curve, measures no loss and makes no claim about scale. The only size contrast is two final models, 7B and 13B, on ChartQA in Table 2. The paper does not discuss it, and two points cannot show the 'predictable' improvement V6 names. The 'quadratic scaling' in Sec. 2.1 is about data-generation cost, not model scaling. It neither tests nor uses the claim; the closest available relation is cites_only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that chart-specific alignment pre-training (raw JSON data), JSON-only QAs and data-driven QAs improve chart understanding. They say CHOPIN LLM 'surpasses the previous state-of-the-art across four benchmarks', although Table 2 places it second on ChartQA. They also introduce a new 20-chart-type benchmark. They draw no conclusion about scaling or model size.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a chart-understanding multimodal model and compares two parameter sizes; it does not reproduce the original language-model loss scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table 2, the 13B CHOPIN LLM scores slightly higher than the 7B on ChartQA after the same three-stage training on 5M synthetic samples: human split 52.28 to 54.11, augmented 87.68 to 88.67, average 69.98 to 71.39. No uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In domain-specialised MLLMs, a larger LLM backbone gives a modest gain on downstream benchmarks (a two-point size comparison, not a scaling trend).

record.problems: Only one pair of model sizes is reported for the relevant downstream comparison; no uncertainty estimates or scaling fit are given. The evidence concerns a specialized chart task, not held-out language-model pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows were left out. The training ablations in Tables A5–A6 vary training data rather than model size and do not measure the behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss or power-law fit.
No controlled comparison of model shape.
No power-law fit in the multimodal or fine-tuning setting.
No scale-performance curve and no relation to pretraining loss; only an incidental 7B/13B pair.
No analysis of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports' plus 'limits_scope' labels on V6 are dropped. A single incidental 7B-versus-13B comparison of fine-tuned chart models, which the authors do not discuss, does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. The ablations in Tables A5 and A6 vary training data composition, not scale, and are correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship across parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters and tokens is studied.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count is reported.
The paper concerns chart understanding, but does not test whether power-law loss scaling transfers to another modality or training regime.

Only ChartQA scores for one 7B-to-13B model-size comparison are reported here; the paper does not test pretraining-loss predictability, fit a scale-performance curve, or assess other downstream task families for this relationship.
No analysis of scaling exponents, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves is reported.

rows.subject: C HOPIN LLM 13B
rows.operation_detail: Compared ChartQA human-split score with the 7B version
rows.note: The reported score is higher for 13B, but a single size pair does not establish a predictable scaling trend.
rows.check: The values are correct (7B 52.28, 13B 54.11, ChartQA human). But this is one size pair of a LoRA-fine-tuned chart MLLM, presented as a final-model comparison, not a scaling test. It cannot show predictability with scale, so it belongs in fits_no_version.

rows.subject: C HOPIN LLM 13B
rows.operation_detail: Compared ChartQA augmented-split score with the 7B version
rows.note: The reported score is higher for 13B, but a single size pair does not establish a predictable scaling trend.
rows.check: The values are correct (87.68 to 88.67, ChartQA augmented). Same issue as r1: a single incidental size pair that cannot bear on predictable scaling.

rows.subject: C HOPIN LLM 13B
rows.operation_detail: Compared ChartQA average score with the 7B version
rows.note: The reported score is higher for 13B, but a single size pair does not establish a predictable scaling trend.
rows.check: The values are correct (69.98 to 71.39, ChartQA average). This is the average of r1 and r2, so it is redundant, and it has the same issue as r1.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: C HOPIN LLM on ChartQA, 7B versus 13B
reader_labels.reason: All three reported ChartQA scores are higher for 13B than 7B (r1–r3), consistent with downstream performance increasing with model size in this comparison.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Only two sizes are compared, so the scores do not establish predictability across a scale range or support a fitted trend (r1–r3).
